content.thinking:
The user just asked me to push the repository to GitHub. My last attempt at `git push origin main` failed with the standard hint that the local branch is not up‑to‑date with the remote: “the same ref. If you want to integrate the remote changes, use 'git pull' before pushing again.” This tells me that the remote `main` has commits I don’t have locally, so a simple push would be rejected.

I need to bring my local branch up to date before I can push my new commits (the ones I just made for the smarter verify‑loop and the freebuff retest). The safest way, given that I want to keep a clean linear history, is to pull with `--rebase`. That will replay my local commits on top of whatever is on `origin/main`. If there are no conflicts, the rebase will be automatic; if there are conflicts, the command will stop and I’d have to resolve them, but the user hasn’t asked for conflict handling, and the repository is small, so I’ll assume the rebase will succeed.

After the rebase I should push again. To keep the output concise for the user, I’ll pipe both the pull and the push through `tail -2` so they only see the last few lines (which usually contain the success/failure summary). Finally, it would be helpful to show the most recent commits that are now on the remote, confirming that the two new commits (`4ec7902` and `2147ee5`) are indeed present. A short `git log --oneline -3` will display the last three commits, which will include those two plus the previous one.

Putting this together, the single Bash command should:

1. Run `git pull --rebase origin main` and capture the tail of its output.
2. If that succeeds, run `git push origin main` and capture its tail.
3. Then run `git log --oneline -3` to show the latest three commit messages.

All of this can be done in one `git` invocation line separated by `&&` so that the push only runs if the rebase succeeded. I’ll also set a reasonable timeout (60 seconds) to avoid hanging. This matches exactly the tool call I need to issue.

Thus the appropriate next step is to issue a Bash tool call with the combined command:
`git pull --rebase origin main 2>&1 | tail -2 && git push origin main 2>&1 | tail -2 && git log --oneline -3`, describing it as “Rebase onto remote main and push”.
